Table 1 presents a detailed breakdown of the cumulative speedup from our proposed techniques in priority-aware action scheduler across different batch sizes with Qwen3-32B and fixed async_factor of 1.5. • Priority-aware scheduling improves training throughput by prioritizing sample groups that are most likely to unblock the next trainer batch. Its benefit becomes more pronounced as the batch size increases, achieving 1.81 × \times and 1.42 × \times speedup at batch sizes of 32 and 64, respectively. Notably, the improvement decrease from bsz 32 to 64 indicates that without priority-aware KV Cache residency, the scheduling policy may not fully unleash its potential. • KV Cache residency further improves performance by reducing unnecessary KV Cache eviction and recomputation for high-priority samples. This component provides substantial gains across all batch sizes, providing a 1.36 × \times performance uplift (from 1.42 × \times to 2.78 × \times ) at batch size 64. It also retains its gains for small batch sizes, contributing a 0.91 × \times improvement (from 1.81 × \times to 2.72 × \times ) at batch size 32. • Request migration provides additional gains by rebalancing high-priority rollout requests across workers and reducing KV contention. In particular, it delivers up to 0.48 × \times (from 2.78 × \times to 3.26 × \times ) speedup for batch size of 64 setting. Ablation study. We further examine whether the key design choices inside the priority-aware action scheduler are necessary and optimized with Qwen3-32B. 1) Length-prediction scheduling policy. Figure 15 . Scheduling policy comparison. We first evaluate the effectiveness of our length-prediction scheduling policy. In this experiment, we keep the other system components enabled, fix async_factor to 1.5, and compare three different scheduling policies. As shown in Figure 15 , the length-prediction policy consistently outperforms the other policies across all batch sizes. It achieves up to 95% higher end-to-end training throughput than action-level policy, and up to 58% than FCFS-based priority policy. (a) Predictor accuracy (b) Predictor overhead Figure 16 . Predictor performance. We then profile the runtime behavior of the length predictor. As shown in Figure 16(a) , the predictor achieves a Spearman correlation ( Spearman, 1930 ) of 0.98, confirming that it reliably distinguishes long requests from short ones—sufficient for priority-based scheduling. Though absolute generation lengths may shift as the rollout policy evolves, the predictor conditions on the problem specification and accumulated trajectory history to capture task difficulty and execution progress, providing informative cues for relative ordering. Additionally, the predictor can also be updated at training checkpoints using recent trajectories to mitigate policy drift, with fine-tuning typically converging within only minutes (More details in Appendix E ). On the other hand, Figure 16(b) reports the average predictor latency and corresponding tool interaction time. The predictor latency is much smaller than the interaction latency, thus the overhead can be effectively overlapped. 2) Priority-aware KV Cache residency. (a) Training performance (b) Cache hit ratio Figure 17 . Effectiveness of KV Cache residency. We next evaluate how different components in VenusRL’s priority-aware KV Cache residency affect training performance. Figure 17(a) and Figure 17(b) compare three cache backends across different batch sizes: HiCache, VenusRL ’s trajectory-aware radix cache with LRU eviction for high-priority samples under memory pressure, and full VenusRL with residency-aware priority demotion. Compared with HiCache, the trajectory-aware radix cache improves end-to-end training throughput by preserving KV Cache state of inflight trajectories and thus increasing the cache hit rate. It maintains a 93% cache hit rate under a batch size of 32, compared with 82% for HiCache, and achieves a 56% speedup. However, the cache hit rate drops to only 79% under the batch size of 64 due to severe KV Cache pressure, achieving sub-optimal performance. VenusRL mitigates this degradation with residency-aware priority demotion, maintaining an over 95% cache hit rate under the same batch size. As a result, VenusRL achieves up to 2.09 × \times speedup over HiCache and 1.58 × \times speedup over VenusRL without priority demotion. The experimental result justifies VenusRL’s design choices of priority-aware KV Cache residency. 6.4. Environment Resource Manager Figure 18 . Deployment Density. Figure 19 . Migration Overhead. Ablation study. In this experiment, we validate the necessity of the key components of VenusRL’s environment resource manager. We colocate sandboxes cloned from the same environment template on one node with 400GB of host memory, and compare three different configurations. Figure 19 shows the maximum number of sandboxes a node can sustain. Native E2B saturates at 100 since it admits sandboxes by their declared memory upper limit.Enabling VenusRL’s sandbox placement (§ 5.1 ) alone, which admits sandboxes based on their actual physical footprint, lifts the node to 743 sandboxes (643% gain). Adding page sharing (§ 5.2 ) further shrinks each sandbox’s footprint,pushing density to 905, 905% compared with native E2B and 122% compared with VenusRL without page sharing, indicating the strong scalability of VenusRL. Sandbox Migration Performance. This experiment evaluates VenusRL’s RDMA-based sandbox migration mechanism. We compare VenusRL with the native E2B’s recovery path and measure the end-to-end recovery latency of both approaches. The baseline pauses sandboxes on the source node, uploads saved snapshot and resumes it on a new node. VenusRL instead pauses the sandbox, migrates its runtime state to the destination node over RDMA, and resumes it there. As shown in Figure 19 , VenusRL recovers a sandbox in 2.70 s, compared with 3.68 s for the native E2B path, a 1.4 × \times reduction in cross-node recovery latency. Table 2 . KV cache management has been extensively studied for efficient LLM serving, primarily focusing on allocation, reuse, and eviction. PagedAttention ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) manages KV caches with page-like blocks to reduce fragmentation, while vAttention ( Prabhu et al., 2025 ) further decouples virtual and physical KV allocation. Other works like Mooncake ( Qin et al., 2025b ) and HiCache ( contributors, 2025 ) extend KV storage across GPU memory, host memory, SSDs, or remote storage.
